trivia: Mother Teresa, the nun famous for her work in Kolkata, came from my people; her family spoke my language. I later renamed my main international airport in her honour.
reveal: Mother Teresa (Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu) and Tirana International Airport Nënë Tereza

trivia: Under communism, parents were pushed away from religious names and chose words from my own language instead, such as Lindita ('dawn'). Today the pendulum has swung the other way: my most popular baby names are Noel and Amelia, and in 2014 not a single name in the top 20 came from my own language.
reveal: Noel and Amelia (recent baby names); Lindita under communism

trivia: In my northern mountains, an old law code, the Kanun of Lekë Dukagjini, let a woman swear before village elders to stay celibate for life and live as a man. These 'sworn virgins' could then head the household, carry a gun and do men's work. Only about a dozen were thought to remain in 2022.
reveal: The burrnesha (sworn virgins) under the Kanun

trivia: Ask someone here a question and watch closely: a side-to-side shake of the head means 'yes', and a nod means 'no'. Visitors regularly order the wrong thing because of it.
My people live by besa, a code of honour that literally means 'keeping the promise'. Once you give your word or take in a guest, you protect them, whatever the cost.

In my southern villages, folk songs are sung in layers: one voice holds a long, droning note called the iso while others weave melodies over it. UNESCO proclaimed this iso-polyphony a masterpiece of humanity's heritage in 2005.
My traditional men's hat is a small, round cap of white felted wool called the qeleshe. Its exact shape changes from region to region, so it once told people where you came from.

Highland women in my north once wore a heavy, bell-shaped skirt built from 13 to 17 strips of felted wool, flaring out dramatically at the back. Under communism it nearly disappeared, and in 2022 UNESCO listed it as heritage in urgent need of saving.
In my own language my name is Shqipëria, often translated as 'Land of the Eagles'. That's why a black double-headed eagle sits on my red flag.
reveal: Shqipëria, Albania's own name for itself

trivia: My language belongs to the same big Indo-European family as English, Hindi and Persian, yet it sits alone on its own branch. No other living language is closely related to it.
My most famous novelist wrote much of his work under a dictatorship that banned some of his books. In 2005 he became the first-ever winner of the Man Booker International Prize.
On 14 March, while it still feels like spring, I celebrate 'Summer Day' (Dita e Verës), one of my oldest pagan festivals. Families swap ballokume, crumbly cornflour cookies from the city of Elbasan.
reveal: Dita e Verës and ballokume from Elbasan

trivia: 28 November is my double celebration. On that date in 1443 my national hero, Skanderbeg, raised his eagle flag over the castle of Krujë to rebel against the Ottomans, and on the same date in 1912 independence was declared in Vlorë.
reveal: Skanderbeg at Krujë (1443) and independence in Vlorë (1912)

trivia: My best-known dish, tavë kosi, bakes lamb and rice under a thick, tangy custard of yoghurt and eggs until the top turns golden.

One of my favourite dishes takes hours to cook: thin layers of batter are spread one at a time and baked under a heavy metal lid heaped with hot coals. Cut open, flija shows dozens of layers fanning out like the rays of the sun.
My capital's signature dish, fërgesë, is a bubbling clay pot of roasted peppers, tomatoes and soft cottage cheese, eaten with bread straight from the dish.
At Euro 2024, my footballer Nedim Bajrami scored against Italy just 23 seconds after kick-off, the fastest goal in the history of the European Championship.

A 2014 football qualifier against Serbia in Belgrade was abandoned when a remote-controlled drone flew over the pitch dangling a nationalist flag. Players fought over it, fans invaded, and the match never restarted.

I skipped the Olympics for 20 years under communism and then went home empty-handed from nine Games. My first-ever medals finally came in Paris in 2024: two bronzes in wrestling, both won by Russian-born athletes, Islam Dudaev and Chermen Valiev, who had recently taken my citizenship.
reveal: Islam Dudaev and Chermen Valiev, wrestling bronzes at Paris 2024

trivia: If there's sage in your stuffing or herbal tea, there's a good chance it came from me. I'm the world's biggest exporter of sage, and my wild hillsides supply most of what America imports.
I'm one of Europe's smallest countries, yet I'm home to more than 3,000 plant species, about 30% of all the plant species found in Europe.
I share Lake Ohrid with North Macedonia; it has existed continuously for 1.36 million years, the oldest in Europe. Its long isolation has produced more than 300 species found nowhere else on Earth.
reveal: Lake Ohrid, shared with North Macedonia

trivia: My 'Blue Eye' spring wells up from an underwater cave so deep that divers have gone down more than 50 metres without ever reaching the bottom. The water stays about 10°C all year.
In 2023 I turned the Vjosa, an entire river system from the Greek border to the sea, into Europe's first Wild River National Park, so it can flow freely forever without a single dam.
reveal: The Vjosa Wild River National Park

trivia: The jagged limestone range along my northern border goes by a name that sounds like a warning: the 'Accursed Mountains'.
reveal: The Accursed Mountains (Bjeshkët e Nemuna / Prokletije)

trivia: The hillside town of Berat is nicknamed the 'City of a Thousand Windows' because its white Ottoman houses are stacked so closely up the slope that they seem to stare out at you all at once.

When the artist Edi Rama became mayor of my grey capital in 2000, he had little money for repairs, so he ordered communist-era apartment blocks repainted in bright colours and bold patterns. He later became prime minister.
reveal: Tirana, painted under mayor Edi Rama

trivia: Gjirokastër, one of my UNESCO-listed hill towns, is roofed in heavy slabs of grey stone instead of tiles. Both my communist dictator, Enver Hoxha, and my most famous novelist, Ismail Kadare, were born there.
reveal: Gjirokastër, birthplace of Enver Hoxha and Ismail Kadare

trivia: My national hero, Skanderbeg, fought off the mighty Ottoman Empire for about 25 years in the 1400s. His goat-horned helmet now sits in a museum in Vienna.

During the Second World War, my mostly Muslim families hid Jewish refugees in their homes and refused to hand them over to the Nazis. I ended the war with more Jews than I had before it began, about 1,800 instead of around 200.
reveal: Albania's rescuers, honoured by Yad Vashem

trivia: In 1967 my communist dictator, Enver Hoxha, banned all religion and declared me the world's first atheist state. Every one of the country's 2,169 churches, mosques and monasteries was closed or taken over, and religion stayed banned until 1990.

In 1997, get-rich-quick pyramid schemes that had swallowed about $1.2 billion, almost half my national income, collapsed all at once. Roughly two-thirds of my people had invested, and the anger tipped the country into armed rebellion.

trivia: My only king, Zog I, is said to have survived about 55 assassination attempts. In 1931, gunmen ambushed him on the steps of the Vienna State Opera, and by some accounts he drew his own pistol and fired back.

trivia: The son of an immigrant from my land discovered how nitroglycerin, the heart medicine, actually works: it releases nitric oxide, which relaxes blood vessels. Ferid Murad shared the 1998 Nobel Prize in Medicine for it.

My paranoid dictator was so sure of an invasion that by 1983 he had covered the country in 173,371 concrete bunkers, about six for every square kilometre. The invasion never came, and some bunkers are now cafés and beach bars.
Private cars were banned here until 1991, and the whole country had only a few thousand. Today Mercedes-Benz is by far my most common car brand, and battered old Mercedes sedans are everywhere.
Almost all of my electricity comes from rushing rivers. In 2025 my renewable output covered 105% of the power I used, a record beaten in Europe only by Norway and Iceland.
reveal: Albania's hydropower, led by the Komani dam on the Drin

trivia: My most famous souvenir is a little concrete-coloured bunker that opens up into an ashtray. It's modelled on the thousands of real bunkers my dictator built, and tourists buy them even if they don't smoke.

Below Skanderbeg's castle in Krujë, a cobbled Ottoman bazaar of about 60 little shops sells hand-woven rugs and kilims, felt hats and copperware. It's one of the most-visited shopping stops for tourists in the country.
reveal: The old bazaar of Krujë, below Skanderbeg's castle

trivia: Travellers often take home bundles of çaj mali, 'mountain tea', a dried wild herb picked on my high slopes and brewed by locals as a warming remedy for colds.
